cf.title: glist: _Generic wrapper for selective dlist/dclist usage

input.subject: glist: _Generic wrapper for selective dlist/dclist usage

verdict_reasoning: The idea is clear, and one reviewer found the macros correct, but the proposal fails at desirability as a standalone patch. It touches only ilist.h and adds no caller, so no build compiles the _Generic dispatch (maintenance-fit-1). The thread names one prospective user, in an uncommitted series, and no second one (demand-1). The proposal gives no number for the memory cost of using dclist in all builds, so the existing type may be enough (already-exists-1).

brief.title: glist: _Generic macros to switch between dlist and dclist
brief.problem: Developers who want a list element count only in some builds, such as MEMORY_CONTEXT_CHECKING, must choose between dclist everywhere, which costs memory in production builds, and #ifdef wrappers around each dlist/dclist call. The author wants this first for list validation in the proposed Proxy memory contexts.
brief.proposed_design: The patch adds glist_* macros to src/include/lib/ilist.h. They use C11 _Generic to send each call to the dlist_* or dclist_* function based on the list type. A field can then be a dlist in one build and a dclist in another without #ifdef at each call site.
user_visible_surface: C API: new glist_* macros in src/include/lib/ilist.h that wrap several dlist_* and dclist_* functions.
author_claims: Calling code needs no #ifdef around the most common dlist/dclist APIs and gains little visual overhead.
Using dclist in all builds wastes memory when the count is needed only in checking builds.
Hand-written #ifdef wrappers would mean a lot of effort, repeated for each user.
glist is meant for fields whose type differs by build, not as a default replacement for dlist or dclist.
No real API in the headers uses _Generic yet, so a separate thread is the place to gather feedback on that.
brief.thread_state: Tristan Partin found the macros correct, asked for a usage comment in ilist.h and suggested the name dglist, which the author rejected to leave room for slist. David Rowley and Japin Li object that the patch adds dead code with no caller and should be part of the Proxy memory context series.
unclear: The patch has no caller. The thread does not say whether the Proxy memory context series will include it or depend on it.
The material does not list which dlist/dclist functions get glist_ wrappers and which do not.
The material does not say how the macros behave with compilers or build modes that lack _Generic support.
The material does not say whether the usage comment Tristan Partin asked for will be added in a new version.
The material does not answer David Rowley's point that a count kept only in debug builds checks only its own tracking.

objections.title: New header API with no caller cannot be checked or maintained
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch changes a dclist_* signature or adds a dlist_* variant and updates every caller. The glist_* macros in ilist.h expand only where they are used, so with no user the build stays green. The first developer who tries glist finds it broken or out of step, possibly years later.
objections.argument: The patch touches only src/include/lib/ilist.h and adds no user. Japin Li could not name an existing place to use it (message #8), and David Rowley asked for a caller in the same series (message #5). The author answers that a separate thread gathers feedback on _Generic as an API style (message #7). That is a reason to discuss the idea, but a committer would likely not take ownership of macros that nothing compiles.
objections.author_must_show: Will the Proxy memory context series carry this patch as its first step, with a caller that compiles the glist_* macros in normal and MEMORY_CONTEXT_CHECKING builds?

critic.reasoning: A macro body is checked only where it is expanded, and the patch touches only ilist.h. With no caller, no build compiles the _Generic dispatch, and message #7 does not offer a caller.

objections.title: New API with no caller and one prospective user
objections.failure_scenario: A committer pushes glist_* into ilist.h as a standalone patch. The Proxy memory context series then changes direction, or drops its debug-only count after review. ilist.h is left with _Generic macros that nothing calls, and every later change to dlist or dclist must keep them in sync, with no caller to show breakage.
objections.argument: The only use named is the author's own Proxy memory context series (message #1). Message #3 says glist is not meant for code that is always dlist or always dclist, and Japin Li could name no existing place where it fits (message #8). David Rowley questions whether that one use is worth having (message #5); message #7 answers him, but nobody else has agreed yet. The author wants a separate thread to collect feedback on _Generic in headers, and so far that has produced no second user.
objections.author_must_show: Which callers besides the Proxy memory context series need a list that is dlist in one build and dclist in another, and could glist ship as a patch inside that series?

critic.reasoning: The thread names one prospective user, in an uncommitted series, and message #8 found no existing place for glist. Message #7 explains the separate thread but adds no second user and does not commit to shipping a caller.

objections.title: Plain dclist or a local wrapper already covers the one known user
objections.failure_scenario: The Proxy memory context code can declare its list as a dclist in all builds, or keep a small #ifdef MEMORY_CONTEXT_CHECKING wrapper next to its only use. If glist goes into ilist.h, every later change to the dlist or dclist API also needs a matching glist macro, for a single caller in a different patch series.
objections.argument: dclist already keeps the element count, and using it in every build costs one count field per list head plus an increment per insert or delete. The author calls this a waste of memory (message #1) but does not say how many such list heads a proxy context has. The point that hand-written wrappers would be duplicated for each user (message #1) does not hold yet, because the thread names no second user and Japin Li found none (message #8).
objections.author_must_show: How much memory does an unconditional dclist cost the Proxy memory contexts in production builds, and which second caller would need the same build-dependent list type?

critic.reasoning: dclist in all builds, or a local #ifdef wrapper, can do the job for the one named user. Message #1 calls the memory cost a waste but gives no number, and the thread names no second user.

refuted.title: Standalone macros with no caller, outside the series that would use them
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer pushes glist_* to ilist.h, and the Proxy memory context series then changes direction or stalls. The tree keeps a _Generic API that no code calls. Each later change to dlist or dclist must also keep the glist wrappers in step, and nothing fails if someone forgets.
refuted.argument: [P8] records a commitfest judgment that macro-only changes are not worth the effort "unless it's part of some larger patch". That case removed a macro, so it is only a pointer here, but its reason matches the point David Rowley makes in message #5. Message #7 answers that a separate thread gathers feedback on _Generic. That does not give the macros a caller, and in message #8 Japin Li withdrew his earlier support for that reason.
refuted.author_must_show: Will glist go in as the first patch of the Proxy memory context series, with a second patch that calls it, rather than as a separate commit?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1, which gives the same failure scenario without the precedent. P8 is about removing an unused macro and lapsed for lack of activity, so it must not be used as support here.

refuted.title: A partial mirror API must follow every dlist and dclist change
refuted.failure_scenario: A developer makes a field a dlist in production and a dclist in checking builds, then needs a function that glist does not wrap. They either add #ifdef at that call site anyway or extend glist. Each new dlist or dclist function adds a third name to keep in sync, and nothing reports a missing wrapper.
refuted.argument: The patch wraps "several" dlist/dclist functions (message #1), and the material does not list which. The author keeps the glist name open for slist as well (message #6), so the macro set is meant to grow with a third list type. The only stated need is one debug-only count in one proposed context type (message #1). David Rowley questions even that need, since the count only checks its own tracking (message #5).
refuted.author_must_show: Which dlist/dclist functions does glist cover, and what tells a developer adding a new ilist function that a glist wrapper is also needed?

critic.reasoning: A missing glist wrapper is a compile error at the first call site, so it fails loudly and the developer adds it then. The commit message limits glist to the most common functions, and maintenance-fit-1 already covers undetected drift.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch adds glist_* macros to src/include/lib/ilist.h, a header that backend and extension code includes.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The glist_* macros mirror dlist_* and dclist_* functions and have no caller that would show breakage.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: A dclist in all builds, or a local #ifdef wrapper, may already cover the one named user.

questions: Will the Proxy memory context series carry this patch as its first step, with a caller that compiles the glist_* macros in normal and MEMORY_CONTEXT_CHECKING builds?
How much memory does a dclist in all builds cost the Proxy memory contexts in production, counted per list head and per context?
Which caller besides the Proxy memory context series needs a field that is a dlist in one build and a dclist in another?
What does the count kept only in checking builds verify, given David Rowley's point that it checks only its own tracking?
Which dlist_* and dclist_* functions get glist_* wrappers, and how do the macros behave with compilers or build modes that lack _Generic?

committability.owner_note: The material does not identify any thread participant as a committer. The owner would be someone who knows ilist.h and the memory context code, and who accepts _Generic as an API style in headers.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the first _Generic-based API in the headers and for keeping the glist_* macros in step with dlist and dclist. With no caller, nothing reports breakage.
committability.author_follow_up: The author answered reviewers in messages #3, #6 and #7 and plans to use the macros in the Proxy memory context series.

not_now.evidence_that_would_change_it: A patch in the same series that calls the glist_* macros in normal and MEMORY_CONTEXT_CHECKING builds, plus either a number for the memory that a dclist in all builds would cost or a second caller with the same need.

priority.reason: The patch is about 5 KiB in one header and serves one prospective caller, the Proxy memory context series. Two reviewers asked for it to be part of that series, where a caller would compile and justify it.

provisional_note: Without the code, the set of wrapped functions and the behaviour of the _Generic dispatch on all supported compilers and in C++ header checks could not be judged. One reviewer found the macros correct in message #4.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Safer hash table initialization macro
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a macro, HASH_ELEM_INIT, that sets keysize and entrysize from a named key member and checks at compile time that the key is the first member of the entry struct. The thread grew into a larger patch series by Jelte Fennema-Nio with new hash table creation functions (hash_make and variants), automatic string or blob key detection, and a foreach_hash iteration macro.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last visible messages are positive reviews and fixes from late January 2026, and no message shows the withdrawal or a deciding objection.

precedents_retrieved.title: Change simple_heap_insert() to a macro
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Heikki Linnakangas, Tom Lane, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the function simple_heap_insert() in heapam.c with a macro that calls heap_insert() with GetCurrentCommandId(true) and default options. The goal was to save one function call.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No one showed a measurable performance gain, and simple_heap_insert() is used mostly for catalog updates. Tom Lane objected that the macro requires GetCurrentCommandId to be in scope at every call site, and that such changes cause back-patching hazards and code bloat. Peter Eisentraut added that macros should be avoided, and he closed the entry after the votes against.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
In general, without a clearly measurable performance benefit,
changing functions into macros or inlines isn't a good idea.

precedents_retrieved.title: Generic WAL compression
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes generic WAL record construction so that it can compute a minimal edit-distance delta between the old and new page images (using an O(ND) difference algorithm), and falls back to the existing bytewise-difference approach when the result is not short enough. The goal is to shrink generic WAL records for access methods such as RUM, where small insertions or deletions shift page contents and make the existing delta nearly page-sized.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch received only limited review across several commitfests. David Steele marked it Returned with Feedback because it still needed review and did not seem a good fit for the last commitfest of PG11. Open points from the visible review included the author's own finding of a large time overhead in one RUM case, and the request to make compression optional, which the author was still working on. Stephen Frost suggested resubmitting for a post-11 commitfest.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Since the feature does not seem like a good fit for the last CF of PG11
I am marking it Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: num_sa_scans in genericcostestimate
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch passes the num_sa_scans value computed in btcostestimate down to genericcostestimate, so that genericcostestimate stops recomputing it differently for btree indexes. genericcostestimate keeps computing its own value for other index types.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane said the two values are meant to differ, so the patch is wrong. btcostestimate counts only the =ANY quals on boundary columns, for numIndexTuples, while genericcostestimate counts all =ANY quals, for the number of heap tuples the scan returns.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If it helps, it's only accidental, because this patch is surely wrong.
We *should* be distinguishing these numbers.

precedents_retrieved.title: Generic type subscription
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pg_type column, typsubscription, that points to a type-specific procedure handling subscript expressions, so any data type can support [a] and [a:b] syntax. It moves array subscripting behind this interface, replacing ArrayRef with a generic SubscriptingRef node, and adds a jsonb implementation.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane's review found that one subscripting function combined three APIs: parse analysis, fetch execution and assignment execution. He also found that the node infrastructure lacked the plan-time handling a generic function call needs, and that routing array operations through a function-call API could slow them, which the patch's tests could not rule out. He suggested leaving ArrayRef alone and representing non-array subscripting as a FuncExpr with a parser callout; the author questioned parts of this, and the CF manager returned the patch with feedback based on these reviews.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Actually, after thinking about that a bit more: you've really squeezed
*three* different APIs into one function.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add information about generic/custom plan to pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a generic_calls counter to pg_stat_statements, so users can see per query how often a prepared statement ran with a generic plan. The plan type is tracked through global variables in plancache.c and read in the executor and ProcessUtility hooks.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch after Fujii Masao found that generic_calls for a utility command started to increment after a PL/pgSQL function had run. The author judged this a bug that could not be fixed during the commitfest. Earlier reviews by Fujii Masao had found other counting inconsistencies and questioned the design, including its memory use and whether plan-change detection was the real need.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It's a bug and regrettably it seems difficult to fix it during this
commitfest.

precedents_retrieved.title: Rename files used for index AMs to less generic names
precedents_retrieved.summary: Rename the generic index AM files so they match the table AM naming: amapi.h to indexam.h, amapi.c to indexamapi.c, amvalidate.c/.h to indexamvalidate.c/.h, and genam.c to indexgenam.c. Module developers would have to switch some header includes.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show the decision. Michael Paquier reported the patch as committed in message #8. In message #9, Andres Freund moved over a discussion from another thread with Tom Lane, whose text is not shown, and proposed splitting genam.h by interface instead of only renaming it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Now obviously we'd not want to split things quite that granular, but it does seem like separating out external interface, systable_*, and AM oriented things into a header each would make some sense.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove dead macro exec_subplan_get_plan
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the macro exec_subplan_get_plan, which no code uses anymore. Richard Guo suggested using the similar macro planner_subplan_get_plan where code now fetches subplans by hand.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane asked whether the PlannedStmt->subplans list was still needed or whether the accessors should use the macro again; the author showed that the list is still used. Nobody pursued the patch after September 2022, so the commitfest manager marked it rejected. He judged that removing unused macros is not worth the effort unless it is part of a larger patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think the conclusion here was that the actual list is still used and
cleaning up unused macros isn't worth the hassle unless it's part of
some larger patch?

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert addition of PGDLLEXPORT in PG_FUNCTION_INFO_V1 macro.
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert addition of PGDLLEXPORT in PG_FUNCTION_INFO_V1 macro.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This turns out not to be as harmless as I thought: MSVC will complain
if it sees an "extern" declaration without PGDLLEXPORT and then one with.
(Seems fairly silly, given that this can be changed after the fact by the
linker, but there you have it.)  Therefore, contrib modules that have
extern's for V1 functions in header files are falling over in the
buildfarm, since none of those externs are marked PGDLLEXPORT.

We might or might not conclude that we're willing to plaster those
declarations with PGDLLEXPORT in HEAD, but in any case there's no way we're
going to ship this change in the back branches.  Third-party authors would
not thank us for breaking their code in a minor release.  Hence, revert
the addition of PGDLLEXPORT (but let's keep the extra info in the comment).
If we do the other changes we can revert this commit in HEAD.

Per buildfarm.

precedents_retrieved.title: Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
Reverted commit(s): Further reduce overhead for passing plpgsql variables to the executor.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This patch does three interrelated things:

* Create a new expression execution step type EEOP_PARAM_CALLBACK
and add the infrastructure needed for add-on modules to generate that.
As discussed, the best control mechanism for that seems to be to add
another hook function to ParamListInfo, which will be called by
ExecInitExpr if it's supplied and a PARAM_EXTERN Param is found.
For stand-alone expressions, we add a new entry point to allow the
ParamListInfo to be specified directly, since it can't be retrieved
from the parent plan node's EState.

* Redesign the API for the ParamListInfo paramFetch hook so that the
ParamExternData array can be entirely virtual.  This also lets us get rid
of ParamListInfo.paramMask, instead leaving it to the paramFetch hook to
decide which param IDs should be accessible or not.  plpgsql_param_fetch
was already doing the identical masking check, so having callers do it too
seemed redundant.  While I was at it, I added a "speculative" flag to
paramFetch that the planner can specify as TRUE to avoid unwanted failures.
This solves an ancient problem for plpgsql that it couldn't provide values
of non-DTYPE_VAR variables to the planner for fear of triggering premature
"record not assigned yet" or "field not found" errors during planning.

* Rework plpgsql to get rid of the need for "unshared" parameter lists,
by dint of turning the single ParamListInfo per estate into a nearly
read-only data structure that doesn't instantiate any per-variable data.
Instead, the paramFetch hook controls access to per-variable data and can
make the right decisions on the fly, replacing the cases that we used to
need multiple ParamListInfos for.  This might perhaps have been a
performance loss on its own, but by using a paramCompile hook we can
bypass plpgsql_param_fetch entirely during normal query execution.
(It's now only called when, eg, we copy the ParamListInfo into a cursor
portal.  copyParamList() or SerializeParamList() effectively instantiate
the virtual parameter array as a simple physical array without a
paramFetch hook, which is what we want in those cases.)  This allows
reverting most of commit 6c82d8d1f, though I kept the cosmetic
code-consolidation aspects of that (eg the assign_simple_var function).

Performance testing shows this to be at worst a break-even change,
and it can provide wins ranging up to 20% in test cases involving
accesses to fields of "record" variables.  The fact that values of
such variables can now be exposed to the planner might produce wins
in some situations, too, but I've not pursued that angle.

In passing, remove the "parent" pointer from the arguments to
ExecInitExprRec and related functions, instead storing that pointer in a
transient field in ExprState.  The ParamListInfo pointer for a stand-alone
expression is handled the same way; we'd otherwise have had to add
yet another recursively-passed-down argument in expression compilation.

precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Rename routines for write/read of pgstats file"
Reverted commit(s): Rename routines for write/read of pgstats file
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit ed823da1289, that has made pgstat_write_chunk() and
pgstat_read_chunk() available for public use.  These routines do not
have a symmetric API definition across reads and writes, with the write
part returning a void status, deferring an error detection once all the
stats entries have been processed with an ferror(), and the read part
returning a boolean status.

These routines are just tiny wrappers around fread() and fwrite(), and
extensions can just define they own routines instead of relying on the
same facilities as the core pgstat.c.  This commit removes their
declaration from the public headers, to reduce the confusion.
test_custom_stats is updated to use its own read/write routines.
Perhaps something better could be designed in the future; trying to do
so for v19 is not feasable during beta.

precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit e21cbb4, as the switch to EVP routines requires a
more careful design where we would need to have at least our wrapper
routines return a status instead of issuing an error by themselves to
let the caller do the error handling.  The memory handling was also
incorrect and could cause leaks in the backend if a failure happened,
requiring most likely a callback to do the necessary cleanup as the only
clean way to be able to allocate an EVP context requires the use of an
allocation within OpenSSL.  The potential rework of the wrappers also
impacts the fallback implementation when not building with OpenSSL.

Originally, prairiedog has reported a compilation failure, but after
discussion with Tom Lane this needs a better design.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent proposes _Generic wrappers over dlist and dclist. [P1] shares only the topic of helper macros, and its withdrawal reason is not shown.

The proposal adds only internal C macros to ilist.h and changes no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog, pg_dump output, psql behaviour or client protocol, so nothing user-facing can break on upgrade. Two compatibility points could not be checked without the code. First, the macros may not compile as C++, but they fail only where expanded and cpluspluscheck would catch a header that uses them. Second, the material does not say which dlist/dclist functions the macros cover. The missing caller belongs to the desirability angle.

The patch adds only C preprocessor macros to src/include/lib/ilist.h. It changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol message or exported struct, so it has no persistent or cross-node state. A struct whose list field differs by build would have a different layout per build, but MEMORY_CONTEXT_CHECKING builds already change struct layouts, and the patch itself has no such caller.

The proposal adds compile-time C macros in ilist.h that pick between dlist_* and dclist_* functions. It adds no SQL surface, privilege, catalog entry, view, or data path that a database user can reach. The count is only kept in checking builds, so it offers no new lever for denial of service or information exposure.
Two objections from the maintenance angle. Correctness of the _Generic dispatch was not judged, and Tristan Partin found the macros correct (message #4).
One objection only: the need is met by the existing dclist type or a wrapper local to the caller, and the shared macros add value only once more than one caller exists.
One objection: no demand is shown beyond the author's own pending series, so this is a not-now case. It is not a rejection of the idea.
